- When sentiment is consistently bearish (0.00 or low) and model forecasts show gradual upward drift, reduce forecast slope; true outcomes often overshoot initial highs then drop sharply.
- If recent auction supply events are frequent (e.g., 2+ per 30d) and supply net is negative, model tends to overestimate price stability — adjust downward by 2–5% for each additional auction.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior 18d mean), model often overcorrects downward — cap forecast decline at 3–5% below peak for 3–5 days.
- When sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish signals (e.g., 1.00/0.00 alternation), model tends to smooth out volatility — increase forecast volatility by 1–2% for 3–5 days post-signal shift.
- If true outcome shows early sharp drop (e.g., first 5–7 days) followed by recovery, model often underestimates early drop — adjust forecast downward by 3–5% for first 5 days.
- For 30d forecasts with high event count and negative supply net, model tends to overestimate mean reversion — reduce forecast mean by 1–3% for 3–5 days post-event.
- If sentiment history shows 1.00 followed by 0.00, model often overestimates bullish continuation — reduce forecast by 2–4% for next 3–5 days.
- When true outcome shows “recovery after dip” (e.g., 70–75 → 78–80), model often underestimates recovery — increase forecast by 1–3% for next 3–5 days.
- For 30d forecasts with low sentiment (0.00) and high supply net, model tends to overestimate price stability — reduce forecast by 2–4% for next 3–5 days.
- If model forecast is flat or slowly rising while true outcome shows sharp drop, model often misses early bearish signal — adjust forecast downward by 3–5% for first 3–5 days.
